verified_metadata.title: A physics-informed neural network method for predicting the remaining life of energy pipelines
verified_metadata.abstract: The safe and stable operation of energy pipelines is directly related to energy supply security and public security. Accurate remaining service life (RSL) prediction for energy pipelines is critical to improving transmission system safety, reducing operational risks, and maintaining stable, efficient operation of the energy supply chain. However, conventional methods struggle with complex corrosion environments, limited data, poor physical consistency, and low interpretability, limiting their practical use in pipeline operation and maintenance. This paper proposes a physics-informed neural networks prediction method synergistically guided by physical consistency and feature confidence. The method uses a convolutional residual neural network as the base architecture and introduces a semi-empirical physical consistency loss function based on normative corrosion mechanisms. By constraining the model through learnable physical parameters, it ensures that both the prediction trends and numerical magnitudes conform to the physical laws of corrosion. Meanwhile, a feature confidence guidance mechanism based on gradient sensitivity is integrated to implement directional constraints on the model's dependence on key corrosion features, enhancing the interpretability of the model's feature-based decision-making. Research results indicate that compared to conventional models, the proposed model achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 9.3% and a coefficient of determination of 0.94, representing the best prediction performance. Furthermore, the model output and physical feature constraints demonstrate excellent physical consistency and interpretability. This model can effectively provide reliable technical support for the life-cycle planning, condition-based maintenance scheduling, risk prevention, and efficient stable operation of integrated energy transmission systems, thereby improving the overall safety, economy, and sustainability of integrated energy systems planning and management.

verified_metadata.title: AI-driven climate-resilient HVAC control: A scalable framework for grid-Interactive buildings
verified_metadata.abstract: Residential cooling systems in extreme temperature regions often operate at maximum capacity for extended periods and creating significant challenges for conventional control strategies. Conventional control strategies fail to manage the extreme diurnal temperature variations (>19°C) and rapid environmental transitions characteristic of these regions, resulting in excessive energy consumption and compromised thermal comfort. This study presents a field-validated framework integrating Digital Twin modeling, Graph Neural Networks, and Deep Reinforcement Learning for adaptive building energy management under extreme climatic conditions. The methodology was evaluated through a 14-month field study across five residential buildings in Hail, Saudi Arabia (BWh climate classification), experiencing summer temperatures exceeding 45°C. The DT model achieves high-fidelity thermal predictions (temperature RMSE: 0.62°C; energy RMSE: 0.35 kWh), enabling realistic virtual commissioning of control strategies. The GNN component models inter-zone thermal dynamics with 0.28°C RMSE for 1-h forecasts, capturing spatial dependencies conventional approaches neglect. The DRL controller optimizes HVAC operations through continuous learning, adapting to occupancy patterns and environmental conditions. Results demonstrate 35.3% energy reduction compared to conventional thermostatic control (95% CI: 32.1–38.5%), while maintaining thermal comfort within acceptable ranges for 92.0% of occupied hours versus 68.2% for baseline systems. Performance remains robust during extreme events, achieving 42.5% savings during dust storms through anticipatory control strategies. Economic analysis indicates a 26.3-month payback period with 143% five-year return on investment. The framework demonstrates scalability potential, with coordinated control across 100 buildings increasing savings to 38.0% through load balancing and demand coordination.

verified_metadata.title: Novel physics informed neural network based power-thermal integrated control for extended-range electric tractor
verified_metadata.abstract: Power and thermal systems are critical components of hybrid tractors, where effective energy and thermal management can substantially enhance both fuel economy and thermal performance. However, the asynchronous control timescales of energy and thermal management may lead to performance degradation under prolonged high-load operations. Thus, this article presents a power-thermal integrated control strategy based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN). First, a bidirectional power-thermal coupling model is established to clarify the mutual influence relationship between power and thermal systems. Then, with the model predictive control strategy of multi-structured physics-informed neural network (MPINN-MPC), a power-thermal integrated control strategy is developed to synchronize power and thermal management within a unified time domain, which can optimize the energy flow distribution, improve the fuel economy, and maintain the critical components within the best thermal states. Finally, the effectiveness as well as performance of the proposed integrated control strategy is verified by using comparative hardware-in-the-loop tests.

verified_metadata.title: Net-zero ready building control: Benchmarking Decision Transformers against deep reinforcement learning for PV–battery buildings
verified_metadata.abstract: The integration of Building-Integrated Photovoltaic and Battery (BIPVB) systems is a critical pathway toward carbon-neutral buildings, yet their optimal control is challenged by the stochastic nature of renewable generation and complex load dynamics. While Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising model-free control approach, traditional value-based and policy-gradient methods often suffer from training instability and lack explicit long-horizon optimization capabilities. This study explores the application of the Decision Transformer (DT) to Building-Integrated Photovoltaic and Battery (BIPVB) control by reformulating the task as a return-conditioned sequence modeling problem. By leveraging the Transformer architecture, the proposed method treats the control problem as a supervised learning task, predicting optimal actions based on historical states and desired future returns (Return-to-Go). We conduct a comprehensive benchmark using the CityLearn dataset, comparing DT against a Rule-Based Controller (RBC) and six state-of-the-art DRL algorithms, including SAC, PPO, and TD3. Simulation-based benchmark results show that the DT agent achieves the lowest operational cost across the tested scenarios, yielding an 18.5% cost reduction compared to RBC and outperforming the strongest DRL baseline. Furthermore, the DT shows competitive and relatively consistent performance under varying initial battery conditions. These results suggest that sequence-modeling approaches are a promising direction for offline building energy control and merit further investigation in broader settings.

verified_metadata.title: A physics-informed artificial intelligence framework for virtual operational data generation to enhance planning and scheduling abilities in expanding district heating systems
verified_metadata.abstract: To address the key challenges in urban district heating network expansion—the absence of historical data for new heat exchange stations, complex hydraulic coupling effects, and inherent system imbalance—this paper proposes a physics-informed generative AI framework for virtual operational data generation. The framework develops a graph theory-driven topology-lag fusion modeling method to accurately quantify the spatiotemporal lag correlation between stations and fully characterize the global hydraulic coupling mechanism; puts forward a Building-Thermal-Informed Liquid Neural Network (BTI-LNN) model with both strong physical interpretability and superior dynamic time-series fitting capability; and establishes a data generation system constrained by both national engineering standards and fundamental physical equations, a design that breaks the strong dependence of traditional methods on historical data. Case studies verify that, under high and low load conditions, the coefficient of determination (R2) between the data generated by the proposed method and the measured values exceeds 0.960 and 0.953, respectively, with the generation errors of water supply flow rate and temperature being less than 1.4 t/h and 0.8°C, respectively. The method thus holds significant engineering application and promotion value.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed soft actor-critic for constraint-aware combustion control of methanol/diesel dual-fuel engines
verified_metadata.abstract: Cycle-resolved combustion control of methanol/diesel dual-fuel engines under dynamic operating conditions is challenging due to strong nonlinearity, actuator coupling, and combustion safety constraints. To address these challenges, a physics-informed Soft Actor-Critic (PISAC) framework is proposed by integrating a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate, an SAC-based control policy, and a constraint-aware reward formulation. The PINN embeds thermodynamic constraints into neural-network training to achieve physically consistent prediction of in-cylinder pressure and combustion indicators, providing a reliable interaction environment for reinforcement learning. Based on the surrogate environment, the SAC agent learns coordinated multi-variable control actions through offline policy optimization. Results show that the proposed PINN achieves a pressure reconstruction RMSE of 3.2 bar, while the R2 values above 0.98 for CA50, IMEP, MPRR, and COVIMEP prediction. Under dynamic operating conditions, the proposed controller reduces CA50 and IMEP RMSE from 0.075°CA to 0.271 bar to 0.026°CA and 0.099 bar, respectively, compared with a conventional PI controller. Meanwhile, MPRR violations are eliminated and COVIMEP decreases from 3.41% to 2.97%, indicating improved combustion robustness and stability. Compared with MPC, the proposed framework further improves transient response and actuator coordination under rapidly varying operating conditions. In addition, the trained policy achieves real-time feasibility with an inference time of 3 ms per cycle. These results demonstrate that the proposed PISAC framework provides an accurate, robust, and computationally efficient approach for constraint-aware combustion control of nonlinear dual-fuel engines.

verified_metadata.title: Machine learning-based multi-objective optimization of hydrogen-enriched water hyacinth biodiesel–tri ethylene glycol monomethyl ether fuelled compression ignition engine with selective catalytic reduction
verified_metadata.abstract: Compression ignition engines fuelled with conventional diesel contribute substantially to greenhouse gas and NOx emissions, necessitating the development of cleaner and more sustainable fuel strategies. This study investigates on a blended fuel strategy that combines water hyacinth biodiesel, tri-ethylene glycol monomethyl ether, and hydrogen enrichment, with urea-based selective catalytic reduction (SCR) for NOx control. Tests were carried out on a single-cylinder engine at 1500 rpm across compression ratios of 12, 15, and 18, and brake power levels of 0.7, 2.1, and 3.5 kW under steady-state conditions with three repeated trials. The work is novel by evaluating waste-derived biodiesel, an oxygenated additive, hydrogen enrichment, and SCR alongside ANN-based prediction and multi-objective optimization in a single framework. Hydrogen–TGMEA addition shortened ignition delay to 7.5 °C A and raised peak in-cylinder pressure to 75 bar at CR 18. Brake thermal efficiency reached 31.28%, 8.2% above the biodiesel baseline, while fuel and energy consumption dropped to 0.31 kg/kWh and 12.8 MJ/kWh. NOx rose to 628 ppm but was brought down to 402 ppm by the SCR system. HC and CO2 fell to 81 ppm and 2.14% respectively. A Bayesian-regularised feedforward ANN achieved R2 values close to 0.99 across both performance and emission outputs. Coupling the ANN with a multi-objective genetic algorithm identified CR 15 and 3.1 kW as the optimal operating point, returning a BSFC of 0.3838 kg/kWh, BTE of 25.46%, CO2 of 2.418%, HC of 100.7 ppm, and NOx of 301.9 ppm, a practical balance between efficiency and emissions for sustainable CI engine operation.

verified_metadata.title: DeepWind: A foundation model for zero-shot wind power forecasting
verified_metadata.abstract: Wind power forecasting suffers from poor cross-regional generalization, as existing models require site-specific retraining and fail to capture the non-stationary, multi-regime nature of wind dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose DeepWind, a domain foundation model pre-trained on a newly curated corpus of approximately 560 billion time-series data points from diverse wind sites across different climates and terrains. DeepWind employs a decoder-only Transformer with a Regime-Aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework, enabling automatic specialization across distinct physical operating states (idle, ramping, and saturation) without explicit supervision. Decoupled Time and Variate Attention mechanisms further enable effective integration of heterogeneous meteorological covariates for improved zero-shot generalization. To benchmark generalization rigorously, we introduce WindBench, an eight-dataset evaluation suite covering diverse climates, resolutions, and operational scales, ensuring no overlap between training and evaluation data to guarantee unbiased zero-shot assessment. In zero-shot evaluation across WindBench, DeepWind-Base reduces nMAE by 20.86% on average over the best competing foundation model and outperforms fully supervised baselines across all forecasting horizons (1–12 h), while few-shot adaptation of DeepWind-Small with less than 3% of parameters updated achieves an average of 5.0% improvement in accuracy over full-shot baselines. The code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/Hexian-2001/DeepWind.

verified_metadata.title: Hybrid temporal fusion transformer and quantum long short-term memory network for typhoon forecasting at a wind power farm
verified_metadata.abstract: Typhoons pose a significant risk to wind power generation and power grid stability, exacerbating wind resource losses and causing substantial economic damage. Therefore, accurate typhoon prediction is crucial for both onshore and offshore wind farms. In this study, a novel forecasting framework, termed the Temporal Fusion Transformer–Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (TFT-QLSTM) network, is proposed to enhance forecasting performance for wind farms, particularly those located in Gaomei, Taichung, Taiwan. The QLSTM component is based on variational quantum circuits (VQCs), which replace classical linear transformations. The proposed framework generates joint 24-h-ahead forecasts across seven typhoon and wind farm variables, optimized via Chaos Quantum Energy Valley Optimization (CQEVO) and interpretable through the TFT's variable selection network. Quantitatively, for the highly volatile wind gust at Gaomei, the proposed method reduces the MAE by approximately 31% compared with the hybrid baseline (TFT-LSTM) and by more than 77% compared with the standard Extreme Learning Machine. These improvements are averaged over 20 typhoon test events and are statistically significant according to the Diebold–Mariano (DM) test. Furthermore, the ablation study demonstrates that the performance gains are attributable to the QLSTM architecture rather than merely an increase in the number of model parameters. NVIDIA CUDA-Q is employed to enable GPU-accelerated simulation of the quantum circuits within the QLSTM component, with quantum circuit execution performed on an NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU.

title: Phase change material-integrated solar heliostat field-driven methane and power cogeneration: Real-data case study optimized by neural networks and swarm optimization from the energy-exergy and techno economic perspective
abstract: Solar energy integration with thermochemical processes offers a promising pathway for sustainable fuel production and energy storage. The growing global demand for carbon-neutral energy has increased interest in solar-driven fuel production, especially synthetic methane, due to its storability, compatibility with existing infrastructure, and role in long-term energy storage. This study proposes an integrated solar-thermal hybrid plant combining a Brayton cycle, Organic Rankine cycle- Thermoelectric generator unit, vanadium-chloride thermochemical hydrogen production loop, three-stage methanation process, and a dual thermal-energy storage system (molten salt/phase change material). This setup enables high-temperature power generation, renewable hydrogen production, and continuous synthetic-methane synthesis under varying solar conditions. This novel solar–thermochemical system, assessed thermo-economically and integrated with machine-learning-based multi-objective optimization, enables continuous synthetic methane production and stable power generation under variable solar conditions. A multi-layer perceptron, trained using features from random forest regression (achieving R 2 >0.99), was integrated with a multi-objective particle swarm optimization algorithm to optimize system parameters. The combined framework maximizing energy and exergy efficiency while minimizing product cost. Under optimal conditions, the system achieved a 1.4 MW power output, producing 287 kg·h -1 of methane, and a production cost of 29.55 $·GJ -1 . In Yuma (Arizona) conditions, the system generates 5.1 GWh of electricity and 999 tons of methane annually, with energy and exergy efficiencies of 42.9% and 53.3%. The thermal energy storage subsystem ensures about 13 hours of continuous operation during adverse weather conditions. These results demonstrate the technical and economic viability of solar-driven synthetic methane production as a scalable solution for renewable energy storage and grid stabilization.

verified_metadata.title: Machine learning optimized integration of a transcritical CO2 heat pump for sustainable and simultaneous heating-cooling in lithium-ion battery electrode drying
verified_metadata.abstract: Lithium-ion battery electrode drying, a pivotal yet highly energy-consuming step in manufacturing, predominantly relies on inefficient electric heating, resulting in significant carbon emissions and energy waste. The concurrent need for high-grade heating for drying and deep cooling for solvent recovery in industrial ovens presents a critical thermodynamic challenge that conventional systems fail to address efficiently. Here, we integrate a transcritical CO2 heat pump into an industrial battery electrode drying oven, exploiting the temperature glide of supercritical CO2 to simultaneously provide high-temperature drying air, recover N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent, and generate byproduct hot water. Using machine-learning-assisted multi-objective optimization with a back-propagation neural network and the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II, the optimal system achieves a coefficient of performance of 3.85, a solvent recovery rate of 90.9%, and produces byproduct hot water at 65.4°C. A comprehensive 4E (Energy, Exergy, Economic, Environmental) evaluation demonstrates compelling practical viability: the system attains a ‌dynamic payback period of only 2.28 years‌ and reduces ‌carbon emissions by 74.0%‌ compared to the traditional electric heating baseline. Exergy diagnosis identifies the evaporator and compressor as primary sources of irreversibility, offering clear guidance for future technological refinement. This work presents a novel industrially viable integration of a transcritical CO2 heat pump into infrared-hot air combined battery electrode drying process, resolving the fundamental heating-cooling conflict through intelligent design and advanced optimization. It establishes a scalable, economically attractive blueprint for deep decarbonization in advanced manufacturing, applicable not only to battery production but also to a wide range of industrial drying and thermal processes.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed sparse regression for multi-energy load modeling of integrated energy system under extreme temperature events
verified_metadata.abstract: With the increasing frequency of extreme temperature events, abnormal fluctuation of multi-energy loads present significant challenges to the accuracy for multi-energy load modeling of integrated energy systems. To address these issues, a model based on physics-informed sparse regression (PISR) for multi-energy load of integrated energy systems (MEL-IES) is proposed to improve the accuracy, interpretability and data requirements of the load model under extreme temperature events for energy dispatch control. An expert database is developed to incorporate diverse dynamic characteristics of the load model, thereby enabling the construction of a control-oriented load model. Specifically, a temperature-dominated comprehensive meteorological index is proposed for the first time to enrich the diversity of elements within the expert database and to facilitate pre-screening of MEL-IES inputs. Subsequently, the double-layer model-based χ2 detection unit is improved to identify extreme temperature events, with the outputs serve as prior knowledge to trigger adaptive regulation of the MEL-IES model. Building upon this prior knowledge, a requirement-driven PISR (RD-PISR) method is developed for MEL-IES. To refine the critical physics-informed elements, the RD algorithm is employed to dynamically adjust the parameters of the PISR model for order reduction and to construct a multi-parameter fitting model, thereby achieving a balance between model simplicity and accuracy. Finally, experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves better performance than benchmark models, lowers data dependence and shortens training time by 52.3%-71.4%. Ablation experiments further indicate that this framework obtains an RMSE of 0.84%, an R2 of 0.973 and the best interpretability.

verified_metadata.title: Building retrofitting towards net zero energy under climate change: Application of a machine learning model
verified_metadata.abstract: The challenge in retrofitting to achieve Net Zero Energy Building (NZEB) lies in identifying the most effective retrofit measures to optimize energy performance and reduce carbon emissions. So far, weather data from meteorological stations have mostly been used in simulations, but these do not account for future weather conditions that may result from climate change. The primary objective of this work is to develop a robust, machine-learning-driven optimization framework to identify climate-adaptive retrofit measures for residential NZEBs across diverse global locations, accounting for both current and future climate change scenarios. Thirty-five combinations of climate zones and time frames are simulated using a machine learning model, leveraging its low computational time. The non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA-III) is applied to the building model to optimize the energy consumption and the predicted percentage of dissatisfaction (PPD), while maintaining NZE balance. The Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to the Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) is then employed to identify a unique, robust optimal solution from the Pareto front. Using future scenarios defined by the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways framework, lower insulation values are recommended for the Fossil Fuel-dependent Future scenario compared to the Sustainable Future scenario, with reductions of up to 20%, 10%, and 13% in climate types C (Warm Temperate Climate), D, (Snow Climate) and E (Polar Climate), respectively. Additionally, the results indicate that building energy consumption and PPD can be reduced by up to 81% and 67%, respectively, compared to the base case through the integration of passive and renewable retrofit measures.

title: CausalHES: A causal source separation framework for weather-invariant household energy behavior segmentation and personalized demand management
abstract: Effective energy efficiency policies and personalized demand management require a clear picture of household consumption behavior. Observed load profiles, however, are heavily confounded by meteorological conditions, which obscures intrinsic behavioral patterns and hinders targeted interventions. This paper presents CausalHES, a deep learning framework whose objective is to learn weather-invariant behavioral representations for robust household segmentation by reframing the problem as a causal source separation task. A Causal Source Separation Autoencoder (CSSAE) disentangles raw load profiles into weather-independent base consumption and weather-dependent effects, enforcing explicit statistical independence between the latent representations of base load and weather through a composite loss that combines mutual information minimization, adversarial training, and distance correlation. Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) then groups the purified base load embeddings, yielding robust, weather-independent segments. On data from 1000 Irish smart-meter households, CausalHES attains 88.0% accuracy in recovering socio-economic household categories, exceeding the best traditional clustering baseline (56.0%), the best weather normalization baseline (60.4%), and the best VAE-based disentanglement baseline (66.2%) by 32.0, 27.6, and 21.8 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of the causal independence enforcement and the architectural separation, and semantic consistency analysis (r=0.78) validates the interpretability of the separated weather component, providing actionable insights for energy analytics and policy making.

title: Renewable energy integration through optimized draft-tube guide vanes for flexible high head Francis turbine operation
abstract: The integration of intermittent renewable energy sources requires hydropower units to operate more flexibly and reliably over a wider load range. However, the flexible operation of Francis turbines, in particular high-head ones, is often constrained by flow instabilities, particularly rotating vortex rope (RVR) induced pressure pulsations under partial-load operating conditions. This study proposes a cost-effective multi-objective optimization framework to identify draft tube adjustable guide vanes (DTGV) configurations that mitigate RVR induced instabilities without compromising hydraulic efficiency under partial load (PL) operation. The framework combines design of experiments, computational fluid dynamics, a back-propagation neural network surrogate model, and a multi-objective genetic algorithm. To accelerate the optimization process, a steady-state mean swirl number is introduced as a practical surrogate indicator for RVR induced pressure pulsations. The close agreement between the back-propagation neural network predicted values and CFD results demonstrates the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed framework. The selected optimized DTGV reduces the low-frequency pressure pulsations amplitude by more than 70% compared to the traditional draft tube. Flow analysis reveals that the DTGV disrupts the main helical RVR into several tip vortices, substantially reduces the tangential velocity and confines flow unsteadiness to the shear layer between the outer and central regions, preventing the RVR formation. These results demonstrate that optimized DTGVs can provide a practical retrofit strategy for enhancing high head Francis's turbine stability and operational flexibility, supporting the integration of renewable energy into power systems.

title: Distributed solar generation forecasting using attention-based deep neural networks for cloud movement prediction
abstract: Accurate forecasts of distributed solar generation are necessary to maintain grid stability amid the increased uptake of distributed solar photovoltaic (PV) systems. However, the high variability of solar generation over short time intervals (seconds to minutes) caused by cloud movement makes this forecasting task difficult. To address this, using cloud images, which capture the second-to-second changes in cloud cover affecting solar generation, has shown promise. Recently, deep neural networks with attention that focus on important regions of an image have been applied with success in many computer vision applications. However, whether such methods provide meaningful benefits for cloud movement forecasting, and how such improvements propagate through to downstream solar generation forecasting accuracy, remains under-explored. In this study, we conduct a large-scale empirical investigation of the impact of attention-based cloud forecasting on solar generation forecasting, addressing a gap that has been overlooked in the literature. To this end, we develop a pipeline that incorporates an attention-enhanced convolutional long short-term memory network and an existing self-attention-based video prediction method to forecast cloud movement using satellite imagery. The effectiveness of the resulting cloud forecasts is evaluated through their downstream impact on solar forecasting across 50 PV sites in Australia. We further provide insights into the cloud conditions under which attention-based cloud forecasting methods yield the most significant improvements in downstream solar forecasting accuracy. We find that for clouds at high altitudes, the cloud predictions obtained using attention-based methods result in solar forecast skill score improvements of 5.86% or more compared to non-attention-based methods.

In this study, we conduct a large-scale empirical investigation of the impact of attention-based cloud forecasting on solar generation forecasting, addressing a gap that has been overlooked in the literature. To this end, we develop a pipeline that incorporates an attention-enhanced convolutional long short-term memory network and an existing self-attention-based video prediction method to forecast cloud movement using satellite imagery. The effectiveness of the resulting cloud forecasts is evaluated through their downstream impact on solar forecasting across 50 PV sites in Australia. We further provide insights into the cloud conditions under which attention-based cloud forecasting methods yield the most significant improvements in downstream solar forecasting accuracy. We find that for clouds at high altitudes, the cloud predictions obtained using attention-based methods result in solar forecast skill score improvements of 5.86% or more compared to non-attention-based methods.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed deep learning for combustion instability diagnosis in an acoustically forced spray swirling flame
verified_metadata.abstract: Combustion instability (CI) threatens the safe and efficient operation of fuel-flexible gas turbines, making reliable diagnosis critical. Although conventional deep-learning models have advanced flame-image-based CI diagnosis, their accuracy remains limited when different states exhibit highly similar visual patterns. More importantly, it remains unclear whether these models exploit superficial image cues or capture the coherent modal dynamics underlying CI. This paper develops a deep-learning framework integrating accurate diagnosis with physics-informed interpretation using high-speed OH* chemiluminescence images of an ethanol spray swirling flame. To our knowledge, this is the first application of a fine-tuned multimodal large language model (MLLM, Qwen) to CI diagnosis. Qwen achieves a mean test accuracy of 99.67%, compared with 97.29%, 98.96%, and 83.69% for CNN, CNN-LSTM, and CNN-Transformer, respectively. POD modal retention and removal are then used as controlled physical perturbations to identify the flame structures supporting model decisions. The CNN mainly relies on medium- and high-order local structures, whereas the CNN-LSTM further exploits their temporal evolution. By contrast, Qwen exceeds 80% accuracy using only the first 10 POD modes, which contain approximately 55% of the fluctuation energy, and is highly sensitive to Modes 2-4, which capture the forcing-induced advancement of longitudinal modes and the redistribution from spiral-like to longitudinal structures. These results show that modal energy does not determine diagnostic relevance and that different architectures rely on distinct physical evidence. Qwen's superior performance is associated with its joint use of coherent modal reorganization and multiscale local flame information. The proposed framework improves both diagnostic accuracy and physical interpretability, providing a basis for active control of low-carbon gas turbines.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed large language model with contrastive temporal embedding for transient thermal-hydraulic prediction in loss-of-coolant accidents
verified_metadata.abstract: Reliable transient assessment during loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs) is essential for maintaining the safety and flexibility of nuclear energy systems, yet remains challenging because the underlying two-phase thermal-hydraulic process is highly nonlinear, rapidly varying and expensive to resolve numerically. This study proposes a physics-informed large language model, termed PI-LLM, for fast assessment of LOCA parameters with limited accident data. The model integrates three complementary components. First, a suffix-aware contrastive embedding strategy aligns textual physical priors with critical temporal segments, enabling the model to emphasize abrupt changes during coolant loss. Second, a multi-scale wavelet convolutional neural network extracts coupled trend and transient features from pressure, flow, void fraction, velocity, density and internal-energy signals. Third, a self-supervised signal-to-text reconstruction module regularizes hidden representations by recovering masked physical variables and their first-order temporal variations. Physics-informed residuals derived from the two-fluid six-equation model are incorporated into the training objective to improve physical consistency. Experiments on a multi-pipeline LOCA simulation dataset show that PI-LLM achieves an average MAE of 0.0027, RMSE of 0.0159 and R2 of 0.9984, outperforming PINN, KAN and Time-LLM baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further confirm that contrastive temporal alignment, multi-scale frequency-domain extraction and self-supervised reconstruction jointly improve accuracy and robustness near accident-induced transients. These results indicate that PI-LLM can serve as an efficient surrogate for real-time thermal-hydraulic assessment and decision support in low-carbon nuclear energy systems.

title: Molten carbonate electrolysis modeling and optimization using feedforward neural networks
abstract: Molten Carbonate Electrolysis enables high-temperature co-electrolysis of CO 2 and H 2 O to syngas, offering an attractive route for carbon utilization and flexible power-to-X operation under variable renewable electricity. However, physics-based performance models often require extensive parameterization and are not readily applicable for rapid screening, control-oriented prediction, or operating-point optimization. In this work, compact feedforward artificial neural networks are developed as fast surrogate models to predict MCE cell voltage from operating conditions using literature datasets. Four single-hidden-layer ANN models were trained in MATLAB using Levenberg-Marquardt learning with Bayesian regularization and dropout: (i) a temperature-current density model with a 2-3-1 architecture, (ii) a fuel-side composition model with a 5-5-1 architecture, (iii) an oxidant-side composition model with a 4-4-1 architecture, and (iv) a combined thermal-flow model with a 9-5-1 architecture, where the notation denotes input-hidden-output neurons. The proposed models reproduce experimental polarization behavior with unseen test-set relative errors on the order of 0.3-0.4% and capture key nonlinear dependencies across the investigated operating ranges. Finally, the combined 9-5-1 ANN surrogate is embedded in a constrained optimization workflow to identify operating conditions that minimize cell voltage at fixed current density while improving electrochemical efficiency, yielding ANN-derived optimal thermal-flow parameters.

title: High-fidelity modeling of pressurized water reactor flow fields for data-driven applications
abstract: This work presents a high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and data-driven modeling framework for assembly-level flow characterization in a four-loop pressurized water reactor (PWR). A full lower-plenum and core-inlet domain was constructed using publicly available geometry and operating conditions, enabling transient simulations with pump-induced swirl boundary conditions. The results show that pump-induced cold-leg swirl and lower-plenum transport generate strongly heterogeneous assembly-wise inlet flow distributions, particularly near the lower core region, while axial resistance and mixing progressively homogenize the flow at higher elevations. These physics-informed datasets were subsequently used to evaluate machine learning (ML) applications for partial field reconstruction and short-term autoregressive prediction. A 3D convolution-based inpainting model successfully reconstructed missing assembly-level mass flow rates from partial observations, with errors concentrated in the highly turbulent base (bottom) layer and diminishing significantly in upper layers. Comparative analysis across multiple ML models demonstrates that spatially aware architectures, particularly ConvLSTM, significantly outperform sequence-based (LSTM) and operator-learning (DeepONet) approaches by effectively capturing coupled spatio-temporal dynamics. The study also highlights key challenges, including the sensitivity of inlet flow predictions to turbulence and mesh resolution, as well as the absence of full-scale experimental validation data. Despite these limitations, the results remain consistent with expected physical behavior. Overall, this work establishes high-fidelity CFD as a critical foundation for developing data-driven surrogates, sparse sensing strategies, and future multiphysics coupling frameworks, while outlining directions for scalable, interpretable, and multi-fidelity learning approaches in nuclear reactor modeling.

title: Data-driven electricity–computing–thermal coordinated optimization for data centers with MDN-based scenario probability updating and ADMM with adaptive common degradation degree
abstract: Coordinated electricity–computing–thermal (ECT) operation of data centers (DCs) can effectively reduce operating cost and energy consumption. However, the dual uncertainty of computing-task demand and renewable generation poses major challenge to highly renewable and reliable DC power supply. To address this critical concern, this paper proposes an online ECT collaborative model for green-power-connected DC. First, the flexibility on the electricity, computing, and thermal sides is jointly exploited to realize the balance between power supply and computing demand. Second, a data driven joint uncertainty modeling method is developed, which combines Wasserstein generative adversarial networks with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) for joint scenario generation, and introduced convolutional neural network trained mixture density network (CNN-MDN) for online estimating the initial probability distribution of joint scenario generation while rolling optimization with observation vectors. Third, a bi-level distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework is developed based on a novel alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) with adaptive common degradation degree, enabling parallel solution of the DC and energy subsystems and yielding optimal decisions from both power consumption and economic perspectives. Case studies demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively exploit multi-flexibility resources, and significantly improve the temporal matching between renewable generation and computing demand. Compared with the baseline case without flexibility, the fully flexibility resources coordinated case reduces the total cost by 29.9% and the total DC power consumption by 9.3%. These results verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework in simultaneously improving the economy, energy efficiency, and operational robustness of DC.

verified_metadata.title: Cross-scale regime-aware physics-informed forecasting for reliable wind-speed prediction in risk-aware wind power operation
verified_metadata.abstract: Reliable wind-speed forecasting is essential for risk-aware wind power operation, but aggregate accuracy can be dominated by normal samples and conceal large errors under gust-dominated regimes. To address this pseudo-accuracy problem, this study proposes the Adaptive Gated Physics-informed Network (AGruPn), a cross-scale regime-aware forecasting framework that links fine-grained operating-condition recognition, regime-adaptive physical prediction, and uncertainty quantification. AGruPn first reconstructs high-frequency wind-speed dynamics from sparse observations, then identifies operating regimes through a cross-scale statistical trigger, and finally activates a gated adaptive physical-guided network with learnable spline parameterization, Partial Differential Equation (PDE)-inspired temporal residuals, Genetic Programming (GP)-based gust closure, and physics-guided quantile learning. Unlike a single global predictor, AGruPn uses the recognized regime to switch the active physical residual and to modulate the interaction between data loss, physical consistency, symbolic gust correction, and interval generation. Experiments on National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), Open Renewable Energy Systems (ORES), Site1–3, Aventa, and Mountain Distributed Generation Test (MDGT) datasets show that AGruPn improves both point and interval forecasting against recurrent, decomposition-based, physics-informed, and contemporary long-sequence baselines. On Site1–3 and Aventa, AGruPn obtains the lowest overall symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) values of 2.709, 2.719, 2.789, and 11.849, respectively. On NREL and ORES, AGruPn achieves SMAPE values of 3.728 and 3.639, improving over the best competing methods by 4.95% and 1.65%. Condition-specific and ablation analyses further show that regime-aware physical constraints improve interval reliability and reveal remaining challenges under high-frequency gust subsets.

verified_metadata.title: An attention-guided residual block-based physics-informed neural network for interpretable SOH estimation of lithium-ion batteries
verified_metadata.abstract: Data-driven approaches are commonly used for estimating the state of health (SOH) of lithium-ion batteries, but their lack of interpretability and high data dependence limit practical use. To address this, we propose ARPINN, an Attention-Guided Residual block-based Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN). ARPINN enhances transparency and reliability in SOH estimation. It uses the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) film growth model to simulate battery degradation and incorporates Deep Hidden Physics Modeling (DeepHPM) within the PINN framework to approximate the partial differential equations (PDEs) governing degradation. The network includes residual block connections to handle nonlinearity and multi-scale aging dynamics. A physics-based monotonic constraint is embedded in ARPINN to relate peak areas of incremental capacity (IC) curves to SOH, ensuring consistency with electrochemical degradation mechanisms like active material loss. Additionally, ARPINN introduces an Initial State Attention (ISA) mechanism to capture temporal features by computing similarity to the initial charging cycle. Combining physical modeling, residual design, and attention-guided learning enables ARPINN to achieve high interpretability. Experimental evaluations on TJU and CALCE datasets show that ARPINN improves prediction accuracy, achieving an average Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of less than 2% across different datasets. Furthermore, extensive validation demonstrates its superior robustness and generalization capability in small-sample learning and cross-system transfer scenarios.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed dynamic environmental footprint assessment and intelligent energy management for PV–heat pump sustainable building energy systems in hot-arid climates
verified_metadata.abstract: Hybrid photovoltaic (PV)–heat pump building systems can reduce fossil-fuel dependence, but their environmental performance is difficult to evaluate when PV generation, heat-pump efficiency, storage states, grid import, and recovered heat vary hourly. This study develops an EnergyPlus–physics-informed neural network (PINN)–adaptive life cycle assessment (LCA)–deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for dynamic environmental-footprint evaluation and control of a PV–air-to-water heat pump (A2WHP)–thermal energy storage (TES)/battery energy storage system (BESS)–hydrogen waste heat recovery (H2-WHR) building system in the hot-arid climate of Najran, Saudi Arabia. EnergyPlus generated hourly reference data, while the PINN provided fast physics-constrained surrogate predictions of PV output, heat-pump thermal output, TES temperature, H2-WHR contribution, and grid exchange. Adaptive LCA converted hourly operational flows into carbon, water, energy, and natural resource footprints, which were aggregated into a normalized Environmental Footprint Index (EFI). DRL optimized operating actions using EFI, cost, comfort, and operational-constraint terms. The PINN achieved R2 values above 0.90 for PV output and 0.99 for heat-pump thermal output, with physics residuals below 12% of system power. Compared with the S1 rule-based baseline, the selected environmental-priority DRL policy reduced EFI from 1.00 to 0.74 and decreased annual operating cost by 18% while keeping comfort violations below 1.1%. Pareto and sensitivity analyses identified cost–environment trade-offs, heat-pump COP, and H2 recovery ratio as key performance drivers. Practical H2-WHR implementation requires short-distance access to low-grade heat through insulated district-scale networks with acceptable exergy losses.

title: Physics-aware deep reinforcement learning for radiant floor heating: A Sim-to-Real framework for proactive energy management
abstract: Radiant floor heating systems present significant thermodynamic control challenges due to their massive thermal inertia, often causing traditional reactive controllers to fail to balance energy efficiency with occupant thermal comfort. This study proposes a physics-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for residential energy management that exploits the building's concrete slab as short-term thermal energy storage. To establish the simulation-to-reality (Sim-to-Real) framework, a reliable 5R3C thermal network model was developed and calibrated via a gradient-based optimization approach. The proposed Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent uses engineered thermodynamic state features, notably indoor temperature gradients and predictive look-ahead horizons, enabling the agent to characterize the thermal mass and execute proactive load-shifting strategies. Furthermore, to accommodate dynamic operational schedules, the framework integrates a lighting-based heuristic proxy for the autonomous generation of adaptive target glidepaths, allowing the agent to execute pre-heating and thermal coasting. Optimized via the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) algorithm, the physics-aware DRL policy demonstrated exceptional robustness in a real-world deployment. Results show that the proposed framework achieves significant energy savings ranging from 9.7% to 14.4% in simulation and 15.9% during real-world online control compared to the conventional bang-bang baseline, while satisfying dynamic thermal comfort constraints with negligible thermal violations. This research provides a scalable and cost-effective Sim-to-Real solution for next-generation building energy management systems, proving that high-inertia residential heating can be optimized as virtual thermal batteries without requiring computationally intensive online optimization.

verified_metadata.title: A spatiotemporal physics-informed deep learning framework incorporating wake interference modeling for enhanced wind farm power prediction performance
verified_metadata.abstract: With the increasing scale of wind farms, the impact of wake effects on turbine safety and power generation efficiency becomes increasingly significant. In practical engineering applications, ultra-short-term wind farm power prediction requires reliable prediction accuracy, generalization performance, and computational efficiency. To this end, this paper proposes a comprehensive power prediction framework integrating physical information and deep learning. By spatiotemporally decoupling the physical process of power generation into three stages of flow field reconstruction, wake topological inference, and power mapping, the proposed framework establishes physics-data coupled models for single-turbine wakes, multi-turbine wake interactions, and power prediction, respectively. To ensure that prediction results comply with the fundamental laws of fluid evolution and energy conversion, the Navier-Stokes equations, the vorticity equation, inter-turbine influence relationships, and theoretical power curves are embedded as physical constraints, enabling the framework to adapt to dynamic operating conditions. Furthermore, a closed-loop error correction mechanism based on transfer learning is introduced to mitigate cumulative errors of turbines, and a gradient-based normalization and loss weight training strategy is adopted to resolve optimization conflicts between data and physical equations, ensuring stable model convergence. Validation based on simulated and measured data demonstrates that the mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error of the framework are 73.67 kW and 3.06%, respectively, with a millisecond-level computational speed. This work provides model support for digital wind farm operations and intelligent power grid dispatching.

title: Physics-informed design of PV coupled alkaline water electrolysis with battery energy storage under fluctuating power through dynamic modeling
abstract: Expanding renewable energy is essential for sustainability, but fluctuating power sources pose significant challenges to the stability of green hydrogen systems. Although PV coupled water electrolyzer systems are often designed using conventional techno-economic metrics, such approaches neglect dynamic electrochemical and thermal responses under variable power operation. This study develops a physics-based dynamic model for a PV coupled alkaline water electrolysis and battery system. The model resolves coupled dynamics across the stack and the balance of plant. Twelve scenarios are proposed to examine the impact of physically informed considerations on system design. Each scenario is evaluated using three decision-making methods, comparing a conventional indicator set with an augmented set that includes physically informed indicators. The conventional indicators include LCOH, curtailment, and battery state of charge variation, while the physically informed indicators include cell voltage variation, rapid O 2 in H 2 rise duration, and system efficiency. The results show that the Const 695 kW scenario held rank 3 in all three methods under the conventional indicator set but fell below rank 10 when the physically informed indicators were included, revealing safety risks that conventional indicators failed to capture. In contrast, the Ramp 695 kW scenario ranked first across all evaluation cases, confirming that a large AWE with a small battery operated to follow the PV output is robust under both economic and safety perspectives. These findings demonstrate that physics-based dynamic modeling is essential for identifying hidden safety vulnerabilities and enabling more informed design decisions under fluctuating renewable power.

verified_metadata.title: Unsupervised early warning of thermal runaway in electric vehicle batteries via a hierarchical multi-scale Transformer and extreme value theory
verified_metadata.abstract: Early detection of battery thermal runaway (TR) is critical for timely intervention and improved occupant safety. However, early TR signals are often weak, and real fault samples are extremely scarce, which limits the practical use of supervised learning. Conventional unsupervised methods, meanwhile, often produce high false-positive rates during long-term monitoring. To address these challenges, this study proposes an unsupervised early-warning framework for electric vehicle batteries that combines a hierarchical multi-scale Transformer (HMS-Transformer) with extreme value theory (EVT). The framework determines the temporal memory length through autocorrelation analysis and captures both transient voltage fluctuations and cross-scale temporal dependencies through a hierarchical multi-branch architecture. Further analysis shows that conventional attention tends to become overly diffused in long-cycle battery monitoring, reducing its ability to discriminate weak fault-related anomalies. To improve thresholding under non-Gaussian residual distributions with pronounced upper-tail behavior, an automated EVT strategy with parameter-stability screening is developed to generate tail-adaptive decision thresholds. Experiments on three months of long-term real-world BMS records with a nominal 10-s upload interval show that, within the available held-out test set, the proposed method detects all three fault vehicles and produces no false-positive warning among the two normal-test vehicles under an EVT-based point-wise decision rule. The first warning triggers occur well before the final valid prediction points of the fault-vehicle sequences, indicating early risk-associated abnormal operating-state deviations. These warnings are intended to support early inspection and intervention rather than direct time-to-TR prediction.

title: Machine learning enabled hybrid approach based on gene expression programming for energy-efficient flexible job-shop scheduling problems
abstract: With increasing awareness of sustainable manufacturing, there has been growing research on energy-efficient flexible job shop scheduling problems. However, obtaining highly energy-efficient schedules remains challenging because the problem is inherently NP-hard and involves complex energy-related operational constraints. Existing approaches often rely either on exact methods, which scale poorly for industrial-sized instances, or on heuristic methods that can rapidly generate feasible schedules but often with high energy consumption. To address these limitations, we develop a hybrid energy-efficient scheduling approach that integrates gene expression programming (GEP), local search, and mathematical programming. Within the proposed framework, GEP is employed to generate machine allocation and operation sequencing decisions, the local search algorithm further improves the generated schedules, and mathematical programming subsequently refines the solutions to enhance optimality. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach consistently yields lower energy consumption than the existing GEP approach, the mathematical programming model, and the decomposition-based approach in most instances, with energy consumption reductions of up to 16.1%, 44.9% and 19.0%, respectively.

verified_metadata.title: FNO-FiLM: A geometry-conditioned neural operator for rapid transient simulation of undulating gas-condensate pipelines
verified_metadata.abstract: Online monitoring and flow assurance of offshore gas-condensate gathering pipelines under sparse field instrumentation depend on rapid and accurate transient simulation. The undulating geometry of these pipelines drives gravity redistribution along the pipe axis, which together with phase change shapes a strongly coupled two-phase transient. However, conventional physics-based simulators rely on fine discretization and empirical closures, precluding real-time use. Data-driven surrogates avoid this limitation but typically learn mappings on fixed discretizations, and existing applications to pipeline transients remain confined to single-phase flow on simple geometries. To address this gap, the transient simulation of gas-condensate two-phase flow in undulating pipelines is formulated as a geometry-conditioned operator learning problem. To solve it, Fourier Neural Operator with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FNO-FiLM) injects the geometric prior into a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) backbone through a dual-path mechanism combining shallow input concatenation with deep feature-wise modulation at every Fourier layer. A high-fidelity transient database is generated with OLGA, covering diverse geometries, boundary perturbations, and initialization strategies. FNO-FiLM achieves an overall MAPE of 0.607% and consistently attains the lowest errors on all five target outputs among eight representative baselines, while delivering three orders of magnitude speedup over OLGA. Even under autoregressive rollouts of thirty times the training horizon, FNO-FiLM reduces MAPE by up to 75% relative to a plain FNO, while preserving resolution invariance under refined grids and keeping errors below 0.26% across four typical engineering scenarios. These results suggest a promising surrogate paradigm for online transient prediction in offshore oil and gas pipeline operation.

verified_metadata.title: Standalone and physics-informed machine learning for inline decoupling of non-ideal biofuel blends to optimize engine control
verified_metadata.abstract:
Biofuels are viable alternatives for climate mitigation; however, their combustion performance varies with feedstock sources and production processes. Dielectric sensors have been used to decrypt fuel blend compositions, transmitting the information to ECU for optimizing engine performance.
In this study, multi-component alternative fuel networks encompassing gasoline, diesel, biodiesels, and alcohols were evaluated across five commercial sensors at 20 °C. Furthermore, moisture stress triggered unphysical multi-phase fluid stratification and hard signal clamping. Eighteen standalone AIML architectures were applied for data processing. While top standalone algorithms like KNN delivered deceptively flawless marks, tracking paths exposed unphysical staircase artifacts across sparse training gaps. Erasing these artifacts via brute-force data augmentation achieved global convergence but imposed severe over 100-fold data penalties.
To bypass brute-force scaling, a physics-informed integrated framework was formulated by integrating piecewise multi-zone calibration curves with a thermodynamic model embedding localized activity coefficients to capture intense non-ideal fluid boundaries. verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed feature reconstruction integrated with selective freezing transfer strategy for cross-domain fuel consumption prediction of heterogeneous ships
verified_metadata.abstract: Accurate ship fuel consumption prediction is vital for maritime decarbonization. However, conventional ships are severely constrained by sparse operational data, while applying conventional transfer learning across heterogeneous vessels induces severe negative transfer due to intrinsic physical discrepancies between hybrid systems containing electrical/battery parameters and traditional diesel ships relying entirely on mechanical-thermal characteristics. To address these data scarcity and negative transfer challenges, this work proposes a physics-informed decoupled transfer learning framework to predict fuel consumption for a data-scarce conventional inland bulk carrier (300 target samples) using operational data from a data-rich modern hybrid tugboat (2500 source samples) under steady-state navigation. First, a Physics-Informed Feature Reconstruction (PIFR) algorithm transforms complex electromechanical coupling features of the hybrid source ship into isomorphic mechanical load feature spaces, eliminating domain differences. Second, a dual-branch attention network combined with an asymmetric selective parameter freezing strategy retains universal hydrodynamic prior knowledge of the source domain while fine-tuning the mechanical feature mapping for the target domain. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates the negative transfer observed in direct transfer, improving ${\mathrm{R}}^{2}$ from a negative value to 0.96 and reducing RMSE to 0.12, outperforming the evaluated machine-learning, deep-learning, and direct-transfer baselines. This work bridges the gap in cross-domain energy prediction between heterogeneous marine power systems under data scarcity.

verified_metadata.title: Multi-objective optimization of biomass and waste gasification for hydrogen production using physics-informed multi-fidelity data fusion and NSGA-II
verified_metadata.abstract: Effective regulation of biomass and waste gasification is crucial for optimizing hydrogen production. However, traditional mechanistic models lack adaptability to complex real-world conditions, and purely data-driven approaches are severely constrained by data scarcity, hindering robust model construction. To address this, an optimization framework integrating physics-informed multi-fidelity data fusion and the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) is proposed to optimize operating parameters of biomass and waste gasification to produce hydrogen-rich syngas. Initially, extensive Aspen Plus simulation data are used to train a base neural network. A Bayesian calibration network subsequently fuses this pre-trained model with limited experimental samples guided by physical rules, significantly enhancing cross-domain generalization and interpretability. Using this fusion model, the NSGA-II is employed to precisely optimize multi-objective parameters tailored to biomass and waste gasification. The framework's effectiveness was validated through three case studies: cross-feedstock application, simulation-to-experiment inverse optimization, and hydrogen-rich syngas production via municipal solid waste (MSW) gasification. Demonstrating robust optimization capabilities, the framework identified optimal conditions for the complex MSW scenario (850 °C and a steam-to-biomass ratio of 1.19), successfully achieving an optimal hydrogen yield of 1.246 Nm3/kg. Ultimately, through comparison with literature-reported experimental results, this framework achieves better predictive accuracy and optimizes hydrogen yield and carbon conversion efficiency, advancing beyond current models.

verified_metadata.title: Experimental investigation of thermal performance and artificial neural network prediction of a phase change material-based battery thermal management system
verified_metadata.abstract: Efficient thermal management is essential to ensure the safety, reliability, and performance of lithium-ion battery (LIB) packs operating under high discharge conditions. This study experimentally investigates a phase-change material (PCM) based battery thermal management system (BTMS) for a 48 V, 10 Ah battery pack composed of 52 cylindrical cells. Thermal behavior of the battery pack was evaluated at discharge rates of 1C, 2C, and 3C under ambient conditions, both without cooling and with cooling using a paraffin wax (PW) base PCM. Key performance metrics include maximum temperature (Tmax), maximum temperature difference (ΔTmax), average temperature (Tavg), and temperature uniformity. Without cooling, Tmax reached 53.75, 56.89, and 58.92 °C at 1C, 2C, and 3C, respectively. With PCM cooling, Tmax reached 48.77, 52.09, and 54.25 °C. Similarly, without cooling, the ΔTmax values were 5.64, 13.58, and 18.7 °C at discharge rates of 1C, 2C, and 3C, respectively. With PCM cooling, these values were reduced to 3.73, 5.81, and 6.6 °C, respectively, indicating enhanced thermal uniformity. Additionally, Tavg declined from 51.21 °C to 48. 86 °C at 1C, with consistent reductions observed at high discharge rates. Temperature uniformity improved correspondingly, decreasing from 2.30 to 1.50 °C. Overall, the system achieved a maximum temperature reduction of 64.7 % under higher-discharge conditions. An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model was developed for temperature prediction, achieving prediction errors within ±1 °C and a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.99. The results confirm that integrating PCM-based BTMS with ANN modelling significantly enhances the thermal safety of LIBs and predictive capability.

verified_metadata.title: Polymer-concrete-rock composite structure for compressed air energy storage caverns: airtightness evaluation and random forest-based leakage prediction
verified_metadata.abstract: Air leakage is a major constraint on the long-term operation of hard-rock compressed air energy storage (CAES) caverns under cyclic thermo-mechanical loading. Existing studies mainly focus on unlined or conventional single-lined caverns, while the coupled response of polymer–concrete–rock multilayer linings remains insufficiently understood. This study develops a fully coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) numerical framework to investigate cavern thermodynamics, deformation, gas migration, and leakage behavior. The framework is evaluated against three complementary benchmark cases representing concrete-lined rock, unlined hard-rock, and commercial salt-cavern conditions. Under the adopted material properties, constitutive assumptions, and interface conditions, the polymer–concrete–rock configuration reaches a peak operating pressure of 14.8 MPa and an average leakage percentage of 0.21% over the 72-h three-cycle period. Relative to the unlined cavern, the average leakage metric is reduced by 63.79%, while the 72-h cumulative leakage mass decreases by 84.4 t (49.62%). Compared to the concrete-rock structure, the leakage rate is reduced by 51.16%, with a cumulative gas loss reduction of 56.2 tons. Furthermore, to overcome the high computational cost and low efficiency of traditional numerical simulations, a Random Forest surrogate model is trained using 72,000 sets of simulation samples, enabling millisecond-level leakage prediction on low-cost hardware. The integrated analysis framework combining physical mechanisms and data-driven methods established in this paper provides a theoretical foundation and technical support for the structural optimization and long-term safe operation of high-pressure hard rock CAES caverns.

verified_metadata.title: Deep Learning-Based Framework for Energy Control and Management in Commercial Smart Buildings and Hot and Arid Climate
verified_metadata.abstract: This study proposes a robust and smart predictive framework for estimating the indoor thermal environment and cooling load demand in a commercial office unit located in a hot and arid climate, during extreme weather conditions. To ensure the generalizability and robustness of the proposed framework, the model was evaluated using onother climatic datasets with temperate highland climate. The office unit consists of five distinct sections with different uses. The framework is a hybrid model combined gated recurrent unit (GRU) neural networks enhanced with a self-attention mechanism to improve time-series prediction accuracy for cooling load demand, indoor temperature, humidity, and residents' thermal comfort. The occupational behavior, along with environmental data and HVAC technical information, was used to enhance the model accuracy. The proposed GRU-Attention model significantly outperformed the standalone GRU model across all prediction tasks. The results showed that in predicting the cooling load, the proposed hybrid model succeeded in achieving RMSE values of 0.5669 and R^{2} of 0.9918 in the concentrated sections, which shows a significant improvement compared to the values of 1.1603 and 0.9657 for the standard GRU model. In addition, in estimating the thermal comfort indices, the accuracy of the model was significantly improved; so that the RMSE for the PMV index decreased from 0.0920 to 0.0580 and for the PPD index from 1.1210 to 0.8900. The GRU-Attention model provides a robust platform for implementing a controller by providing highly accurate predictions with minimal noise. This approach can lead to energy savings, which is a fundamental step towards realizing net-zero carbon buildings and improving energy resilience in smart urban contexts.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed circumferential graph variational autoencoder for exhaust gas temperature anomaly detection in gas turbines
verified_metadata.abstract: Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) anomaly detection is essential for monitoring gas turbine hot components. However, distinguishing condition-induced EGT fluctuations from weak fault deviations remains challenging. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware physics-informed circumferential graph variational autoencoder (PICG-VAE) for EGT anomaly detection. Operating-condition and historical EGT measurements are independently encoded and fused within the variational latent space. A hybrid EGT graph combines the fixed circumferential topology with a learnable adjacency matrix. Physics-informed circumferential structure loss and spectral consistency loss are designed to preserve local circumferential gradients and multiscale spectral characteristics. Uncertainty-normalized residuals are adopted as the monitoring statistic for anomaly detection. Across eight independent runs, PICG-VAE achieves a false alarm rate of 0.86 ± 0.42% and an average recall at 5°C (AR@5°C) fault magnitude of 91.8 ± 3.95%. Ablation studies identify graph modeling as the most influential architectural component, with its removal reducing AR@5°C by 51.6 percentage points. The learnable graph connectivity improves AR@5°C by 16.0 percentage points with only a 0.5% increase in parameters. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, PICG-VAE improves average recall by 2.5 percentage points, and reduces parameters by 36.56%. Additionally, PICG-VAE can adapt to gas turbines with different numbers of EGT sensors. Overall, PICG-VAE balances weak-anomaly sensitivity, false-alarm control, and efficiency.

verified_metadata.title: Thermal-safety-constrained cooling energy optimization for data centers using a physics-informed graph surrogate model
verified_metadata.abstract: The rapid growth of data center electricity demand has increased the need for energy-efficient cooling operation while maintaining local thermal safety. However, high-fidelity thermal simulation is computationally expensive, and purely data-driven surrogate models often neglect the physical topology of rack-level heat transfer and air supply paths. To address this issue, this study proposes a thermal-safety-constrained cooling energy optimization framework for non-uniformly loaded data centers. A physics-informed thermal graph is constructed to explicitly represent rack operating states, adjacent rack thermal coupling, and directed air-supply relationships from cooling units. Based on high-fidelity thermal environment simulations, a graph neural network surrogate is developed to rapidly estimate rack-level outlet temperature distributions and hotspot risks. The trained surrogate is further embedded into a differential-evolution-based optimization framework to identify energy-efficient cooling setpoints under rack outlet temperature constraints. The results show that the proposed surrogate achieves accurate rack-level temperature estimation, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.379 °C and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.523 °C. Compared with the baseline operation, the optimized cooling strategy reduces the average local power usage effectiveness (PUE) from 1.798 to 1.603, corresponding to an energy efficiency improvement of 10.82%, an average daily electricity saving of 255.3 kWh, and a carbon emission reduction of 148.3 kg CO2. The proposed framework provides a fast and physically interpretable tool for cooling energy management and local thermal safety control in data centers.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-informed safe reinforcement learning with adaptive PID–Lagrangian control for long-term cascade reservoir scheduling
verified_metadata.abstract: Cascade hydropower scheduling under stochastic inflows requires coordinated generation decisions subject to coupled hydraulic and operational constraints. This study develops PI–RPPO–PID by adapting and integrating established physics-informed action projection, recurrent proximal policy optimization, and PID-Lagrangian regulation for sequential cascade-reservoir scheduling. A normalized pre-projection Safety Cost aggregates the constraint violations implied by raw policy actions across reservoirs and constraint categories, retaining a learning signal even when action projection corrects the executed decisions. The framework is assessed using the lower Jinsha River cascade through staged parameter screening, multi-seed algorithm comparisons, fixed-multiplier comparisons, and frozen-policy replay under observed and empirical-frequency inflows. Under the evaluated settings, RPPO achieves lower pre-projection constraint pressure and higher incremental generation than feedforward PPO. Adaptive PID regulation meets the prescribed Cost target while retaining substantial generation benefits relative to the three selected fixed-multiplier settings. Historical replay and additional P01 and P99 scenarios illustrate dispatch responses under interannual variability and extreme frequency-based inflow conditions. Executed-dispatch compliance is assessed separately from pre-projection Cost attainment. These findings demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively integrates physical constraint handling, temporal policy learning, and adaptive constraint regulation, providing an effective and interpretable approach to safe cascade hydropower scheduling under the investigated stochastic inflow conditions.

verified_metadata.title: Physics-guided feature synergy transformer for battery state of health estimation
verified_metadata.abstract: Accurately estimating the state of health (SOH) is paramount for ensuring the safety and reliability of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). While existing methods employ multiple health features (HFs) for battery SOH estimation, their generalization across varying operating conditions and chemical compositions remains limited, as the synergistic interactions among these features are often neglected. To address these limitations, a physics-guided feature synergy transformer (PGFS-Former) is proposed for robust and interpretable SOH estimation with a multi-feature fusion strategy. Specifically, degradation-informed and physically interpretable HFs, including the constant current (CC) charging time, the mean CC charging voltage, and the peak value of the incremental capacity (IC) curve, are selected to provide physics guidance at the feature-construction level. In PGFS-Former, an adaptive feature fusion module initialized with the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) is designed to dynamically integrate multiple features during model training, while the multi-head cross-attention (MHCA) mechanism is responsible for capturing the complex synergistic interactions among HFs. The PCC algorithm is used to quantify the linear association between each feature and the SOH of LIBs for initializing the feature weights, thereby providing a transparent and statistically informed starting point for subsequent data-driven optimization. The comparative experiments and ablation experiments on batteries across different chemical compositions and charge-discharge protocols are conducted to demonstrate the performance of PGFS-Former for battery SOH estimation.

verified_metadata.title: A method for quantifying fuel cell degradation power loss mechanisms based on an identifiability-driven physics-informed neural network
verified_metadata.abstract: The output power of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC) decreases after long-term operation. Existing diagnostic methods require shutdown testing or dedicated equipment, which severely disrupts production operations; consequently, the entire stack is often replaced directly in engineering practice, resulting in substantial economic waste. To address these issues, this paper proposes an identifiability-driven physics-informed neural network (ID-PINN) method. Specifically, a multi-mechanism coupled electrochemical model covering five degradation pathways is embedded as a differentiable physics-constrained layer. A dual-branch architecture comprising a monotonic baseline and operating-condition residuals separates irreversible aging from operating-condition disturbances, identifies the evolutionary trajectories of 5 degradation-sensitive parameters using only routine operational data, and decomposes mechanism-level power losses under a unified rated operating condition. Validation using 994.88 h of long-term test data from an in-house stack and a public dataset from Tongji University shows that the test-segment voltage-prediction MAPEs of the two datasets are 1.89% and 1.39%, respectively. The ohmic, activation, and mass-transfer degradation trends reflected by 83 measured impedance spectra are consistent with the model identification results. The cumulative stack power loss is approximately 282.84 W, of which the model attributes 92.2% to catalyst activity decay, providing priority directions for stack inspection and maintenance.
